Press enter or click to view image in full size The interface was only one part of the job. Building the product meant learning to see everything around it. One day, I looked at the tabs open on my screen: Figma, Xcode, App Store Connect, analytics, Product Hunt, Medium, and Reddit. My job title still said Product Designer. My browser suggested something much harder to define. I hadn’t abandoned design. But somewhere between building prototypes with AI, watching users move through a funnel, testing App Store copy, and trying to find distribution channels, the boundary around my job had disappeared. I was still designing interfaces. I was also researching problems, making product decisions, building working prototypes, thinking about monetization, studying analytics, and trying to understand why someone would discover a product in the first place. The title had stayed the same. The responsibility behind it had not. The Interface Was Only One Part of the Product For a long time, I could see the boundaries of my work clearly. There was a user problem, a flow to improve, a feature to design, or an interface to refine. I could map the journey, test the interaction, prepare the screens, and work with developers to bring them to life. The work was never only visual. Good product design has always required research, prioritization, collaboration, and an understanding of user behavior. Still, the interface was where most of my responsibility became visible. It was the part I could point to and say, “This is what I designed.” Building my own products changed that. When I started working on Dayli, Tody, and Ruly, there was no clean handoff between design and everything that came next. A decision made in Figma followed me into development. A line of copy affected the App Store page. A product limitation changed the monetization model. A feature that made sense in isolation created another question somewhere else in the funnel. There was no longer a moment when I could simply deliver the screens and step away. The interface was still important. It was simply no longer enough to tell me whether the product was working. AI Made Building Easier — and Decisions Harder AI-assisted tools reduced the distance between an idea and a working product. I could move from a rough concept to a functional prototype quickly, test an interaction, change the logic, and eventually work directly with Swift instead of waiting for every technical question to be answered by someone else. That freedom was real. For the first time, I could take an idea much further without needing a full team around it. But easier production did not produce easier product decisions. It produced more of them. When almost any idea can become a prototype, the difficult question is no longer, “Can I build this?” It is, “Does this deserve to be built?” Every new possibility created another choice: Is this feature solving a real problem or just making the product look more complete? Should I improve the onboarding or reconsider the value proposition? Is the current version too limited, or is that limitation the reason the product is clear? Should I keep improving the product or spend that time helping people discover it? Is a result weak because of the experience, the positioning, the audience, or the channel? AI made execution faster, but it also made poor decisions cheaper to execute. That changed the value of my experience. Knowing how to produce an interface was no longer the main constraint. Judgment — what to pursue, what to test, what to remove, and when to stop — became more important. The ability to build more things made choosing what not to build a bigger part of design. A Working Feature Is Not a Working Product Shipping my own products exposed a distinction I had understood intellectually but had never felt this directly: A feature can work perfectly while the product around it is failing. Press enter or click to view image in full size A polished interface cannot compensate for a product that people cannot discover, understand, or return to. An onboarding flow can be clear without creating activation. A product can solve a problem without giving people a reason to return. Users can like an idea without wanting to pay for it. An app can be useful and still remain invisible. This is where my design process began to expand across the entire funnel. I was no longer asking only whether someone could complete a task. I also had to ask: How would they discover the product? Would they understand its value from the App Store page? What would make the first session meaningful? What would give them a reason to return? At what point would paying feel justified? Why would they tell someone else about it? These questions changed what I designed. App Store optimization forced me to explain a product before someone experienced it. Analytics forced me to compare my intentions with actual behavior. Product Hunt showed me how quickly a new product has to become interesting to a stranger. Writing on Medium made me articulate the thinking behind the products.
